questions.explanation: SA 706 permits an Emphasis of Matter paragraph to draw attention to a matter appropriately presented or disclosed that is fundamental to users' understanding, such as a major catastrophe. The paragraph states that the opinion is not modified in respect of the matter. A qualified opinion is inappropriate since there is no misstatement or limitation.

questions.question_text: Which of the following matters would ordinarily be communicated in an Other Matter paragraph under SA 706?

options.A: A statement that the report is intended solely for a specified user and should not be distributed to other parties
options.B: A material uncertainty about going concern that is adequately disclosed
options.C: A note in the financial statements on a major post-balance sheet catastrophe
options.D: A material misstatement of trade receivables

questions.explanation: An Other Matter paragraph refers to a matter not presented or disclosed in the financial statements that is relevant to users' understanding of the audit, the auditor's responsibilities or the report, such as restriction on distribution or use. A disclosed catastrophe is dealt with by an EOM, going concern by a separate section under SA 570, and a misstatement by a modified opinion.

questions.question_text: After accepting the engagement, the management of Tara Pumps Ltd. imposes a limitation on the scope of the audit that the auditor believes is likely to result in a disclaimer of opinion. Under SA 705, the auditor shall FIRST:

options.A: Accept a written representation in place of the restricted evidence
options.B: Issue a qualified opinion without informing those charged with governance
options.C: Request management to remove the limitation
options.D: Withdraw from the engagement immediately without discussion

questions.explanation: SA 705 requires that if management imposes a limitation after acceptance that is likely to result in a qualified opinion or disclaimer, the auditor shall request management to remove it. If management refuses, the auditor communicates with those charged with governance, determines whether alternative procedures are possible and, if pervasive effects remain, withdraws where practicable and legally permitted or disclaims an opinion.

questions.question_text: The Companies (Auditor's Report) Order (CARO) is issued by the Central Government under which provision of the Companies Act, 2013?

options.A: Section 143(11)
options.B: Section 141(3)
options.C: Section 144
options.D: Section 139(1)

questions.explanation: Section 143(11) empowers the Central Government, in consultation with the National Financial Reporting Authority, to direct that the auditor's report on specified classes of companies include a statement on prescribed matters; CARO is issued under this power. Section 139 deals with appointment, section 141 with eligibility and qualifications and section 144 with services auditors cannot render.

questions.question_text: Which of the following matters is required to be reported by the auditor under CARO?

options.A: Whether the company's marketing strategy is likely to succeed
options.B: Whether the company's CSR projects have achieved their social impact
options.C: Whether the directors' remuneration is reasonable compared with market benchmarks
options.D: Whether the title deeds of immovable properties disclosed in the financial statements are held in the name of the company

questions.explanation: CARO requires reporting on specified matters such as property, plant and equipment records, physical verification and whether title deeds of immovable properties are held in the company's name. The auditor does not report on the commercial wisdom of strategy, the reasonableness of pay against market benchmarks or the social impact of CSR projects.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is reported by the auditor of a company under section 143(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, rather than under CARO?

options.A: Whether the company maintains proper records showing quantitative details of property, plant and equipment
options.B: Whether any director is disqualified from being appointed as a director under section 164(2)
options.C: Whether the company has defaulted in repayment of loans or interest to any lender
options.D: Whether physical verification of inventory has been conducted at reasonable intervals by management

questions.explanation: Section 143(3) requires the auditor to state, among other things, whether any director is disqualified under section 164(2), whether proper books are kept, and on the adequacy of internal financial controls. The quantitative records of PPE, physical verification of inventory and defaults in repayment of loans are matters covered by CARO.

questions.topic: Special Features of Audit of Different Type of Entities
questions.question_text: The duties and powers of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India are laid down in:

options.A: The Chartered Accountants Act, 1949
options.B: The Comptroller and Auditor General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971
options.C: The Banking Regulation Act, 1949
options.D: The Companies Act, 2013

questions.explanation: Article 148 of the Constitution provides for the appointment of the CAG, and Article 149 provides that the CAG shall perform duties and exercise powers prescribed by Parliament. Parliament enacted the CAG's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 for this purpose.

questions.topic: Special Features of Audit of Different Type of Entities
questions.question_text: In the audit of a government department, the auditor examines whether expenditure incurred was not prima facie more than the occasion demanded and whether public money was used for the benefit of a particular person. This is known as:

options.A: Performance audit
options.B: Audit against provision of funds
options.C: Propriety audit
options.D: Audit against rules and orders

questions.explanation: Propriety audit looks beyond legality to whether expenditure meets canons of financial propriety: no more than the occasion demands, exercising the same vigilance as a person of ordinary prudence would with his own money, no sanction for one's own benefit, and public money not used for a particular person or section. It is an important feature of government audit.

questions.topic: Special Features of Audit of Different Type of Entities
questions.question_text: Performance audit in government organisations primarily examines:

options.A: Only whether expenditure is supported by vouchers
options.B: Whether programmes and activities are carried out with economy, efficiency and effectiveness
options.C: Only the arithmetical accuracy of accounts
options.D: Whether the department has earned a profit

questions.explanation: Performance audit assesses whether government programmes, schemes and organisations achieve their objectives economically, efficiently and effectively (the three Es). It goes beyond regularity and propriety to evaluate results against intended outcomes.

questions.topic: Special Features of Audit of Different Type of Entities
questions.question_text: Under section 139(5) of the Companies Act, 2013, the statutory auditor of a government company (other than its first auditor) is appointed by:

options.A: The Board of directors, within 30 days of the AGM
options.B: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India, within 180 days from the commencement of the financial year
options.C: The Central Government, within 60 days of the year-end
options.D: The shareholders at the AGM, for a term of five years

questions.explanation: Section 139(5) provides that in a government company, or a company owned or controlled directly or indirectly by the Central and/or State Governments, the auditor is appointed by the CAG within 180 days from the commencement of the financial year. The appointed auditor holds office till the conclusion of the AGM.

questions.topic: Special Features of Audit of Different Type of Entities
questions.question_text: The statutory auditor of Bharat Utilities Ltd., a government company, submits the audit report. Under section 143(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, the CAG may:

options.A: At any time, order the auditor to withdraw and reissue the report
options.B: Within 60 days of receiving the audit report, conduct a supplementary audit and comment upon or supplement the audit report
options.C: Within 180 days, replace the auditor's report with its own opinion
options.D: Only conduct a test audit, without making any comments

questions.explanation: Section 143(6) permits the CAG, within 60 days from the date of receipt of the audit report, to conduct a supplementary audit through persons authorised by it, and to comment upon or supplement the audit report. Such comments are sent by the company to every person entitled to copies of audited financial statements and placed before the annual general meeting. Test audit is separately provided for in section 143(7).

questions.topic: Special Features of Audit of Different Type of Entities
questions.question_text: Which of the following is a typical feature of the audit of a local body such as a municipal corporation?

options.A: Checking that expenditure is within the budget sanctioned and incurred in accordance with the applicable Act, rules and bye-laws
options.B: Ensuring that the local body pays dividends to citizens
options.C: Issuing an opinion under SA 701 on key audit matters
options.D: Verifying that the local body has earned a return on equity

questions.explanation: Local bodies operate under statutes and budgets approved by their councils. Their audit typically checks budgetary control, sanctions, compliance with the governing Act and rules, collection of revenues such as taxes and fees, and proper use of grants. Profit, return on equity and dividends are not relevant objectives for such bodies.

questions.topic: Special Features of Audit of Different Type of Entities
questions.question_text: Akshar Foundation, an NGO, receives a grant from a donor agency to be used exclusively for a rural literacy project. The auditor's key concern regarding this grant is to verify that:

options.A: The grant has been treated as general revenue available for any activity
options.B: The grant has been distributed among the trustees
options.C: The grant has been utilised for the specified purpose in accordance with the grant conditions and is accounted for separately
options.D: The grant has been invested in shares to generate returns

questions.explanation: Restricted grants must be used only for the purposes and under the conditions specified by the donor. The auditor examines the grant agreement, separate accounting for restricted funds, utilisation certificates and supporting documents for expenditure. Treating restricted funds as general income or diverting them would breach the conditions.

questions.topic: Special Features of Audit of Different Type of Entities
questions.question_text: A distinctive feature of the audit of co-operative societies under many State Co-operative Societies Acts is that the auditor:

options.A: Is required to report Key Audit Matters under SA 701
options.B: Classifies the society into an audit class based on its working and performance
options.C: Is always appointed by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India
options.D: Issues a report only on internal financial controls

questions.explanation: Co-operative audit is governed by the relevant State Co-operative Societies Act and rules (or the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, 2002 for multi-State societies). A typical special requirement is the award of an audit classification (for example, classes such as A, B, C and D, with the classes and criteria varying from State to State) based on criteria such as financial position, management and recovery performance. The CAG does not appoint co-operative auditors, SA 701 is aimed at listed entities, and reporting on internal financial controls alone is not the function of a co-operative audit.

questions.topic: Special Features of Audit of Different Type of Entities
questions.question_text: In the audit of a co-operative credit society, the auditor finds loans given to members in excess of the limits in the society's bye-laws. This should be:

options.A: Reported in the audit report or audit memorandum as a non-compliance with the bye-laws
options.B: Reported only to the borrowing members
options.C: Ignored, because bye-laws are internal rules of no audit relevance
options.D: Adjusted by the auditor by reducing the loan balances in the books

questions.explanation: A special feature of co-operative audit is the examination of compliance with the Co-operative Societies Act, rules and the society's bye-laws, including restrictions on loans to members. Non-compliance is reported in the audit report or memorandum. The auditor does not make entries in the books.

questions.topic: Special Features of Audit of Different Type of Entities
questions.question_text: Under the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008 and the rules made under it, which of the following persons would NOT be eligible for appointment as auditor of a Limited Liability Partnership whose accounts are required to be audited?

options.A: A firm of Chartered Accountants in which all partners are in practice
options.B: A Chartered Accountant in full-time practice with no relationship with the LLP
options.C: A partner or employee of that LLP
options.D: A Chartered Accountant who audits other unrelated LLPs

questions.explanation: Under the LLP Rules, 2009, the accounts of an LLP that are required to be audited must be audited by chartered accountants in practice. A partner or employee of the LLP, or a person who is a partner of, or in the employment of, such a partner or employee, is not eligible to be its auditor, because the auditor would be examining accounts of a business in which he is involved. A practising chartered accountant or a firm of practising chartered accountants with no such relationship can be appointed, and auditing other unrelated LLPs is no bar.

questions.topic: Special Features of Audit of Different Type of Entities
questions.question_text: In the audit of a partnership firm, the document the auditor should study first to understand the rights and obligations of partners, such as profit-sharing ratio and interest on capital, is:

options.A: The partnership deed
options.B: The memorandum of association
options.C: The bye-laws of the firm
options.D: The register of members

questions.explanation: A partnership firm is governed by the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 and its partnership deed. The deed sets out capital contributions, profit-sharing ratio, interest on capital and drawings, salaries and other terms that the auditor must verify. The memorandum of association and register of members relate to companies.

questions.topic: Special Features of Audit of Different Type of Entities
questions.question_text: During the audit of a government department, the auditor finds that a purchase was sanctioned by an officer whose delegated financial powers were lower than the value of the purchase. This finding relates primarily to:

options.A: Performance audit, since the purchase may not be economical
options.B: Audit against provision of funds, since the budget was exceeded
options.C: Audit against sanction, since the expenditure was not sanctioned by the competent authority
options.D: Propriety audit, since the officer may have benefited personally

questions.explanation: Audit against sanction verifies that every item of expenditure is sanctioned, either specially or generally, by an authority competent to do so. Here, the sanctioning officer lacked the delegated power, so the expenditure is irregular. There is no indication of personal benefit or budget excess in the facts.

questions.question_text: The statutory auditor of a banking company is appointed in accordance with:

options.A: Section 30 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, with the previous approval of the Reserve Bank of India
options.B: Article 148 of the Constitution of India
options.C: The Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, by the Institute's Council
options.D: Section 139 of the Companies Act, 2013, by the board of directors alone

questions.explanation: Section 30 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 requires the balance sheet and profit and loss account of a banking company to be audited by a person duly qualified to be an auditor of companies, and the appointment is made with the previous approval of the RBI. The RBI may also direct special audits.

questions.question_text: Under the RBI prudential norms, a term loan becomes a non-performing asset when:

options.A: Interest and/or an instalment of principal remains overdue for a period of more than 90 days
options.B: The loan is not renewed on the review date
options.C: Interest remains unpaid for 30 days
options.D: The borrower's credit rating is downgraded

questions.explanation: Under RBI's income recognition and asset classification norms, a term loan is a non-performing asset where interest and/or an instalment of principal remains overdue for more than 90 days. Rating downgrades or review delays may be warning signals but do not by themselves define an NPA.

questions.question_text: A borrowal account of a bank became a non-performing asset on 30 June 2024 and has remained NPA continuously since then, with no upgradation. The security is fully realisable at its book value and no loss has been identified by the bank, the auditor or RBI inspectors. Under the RBI prudential norms on asset classification, what is its classification as at 31 March 2026?

options.A: Standard asset
options.B: Loss asset
options.C: Sub-standard asset
options.D: Doubtful asset (doubtful for up to one year, D1)

questions.explanation: Under RBI norms, an asset is sub-standard if it has remained NPA for a period less than or equal to 12 months; here, from 30 June 2024 to 30 June 2025. An asset that has remained in the sub-standard category for 12 months becomes doubtful, so the account became doubtful on 30 June 2025. From 30 June 2025 to 31 March 2026 it has been doubtful for 9 months, which is within one year, so it is D1. It is not a loss asset because no loss has been identified and the security is realisable, and it cannot be standard while it remains NPA.

questions.question_text: Under RBI norms, a cash credit or overdraft account is treated as 'out of order' when:

options.A: The outstanding balance remains continuously in excess of the sanctioned limit or drawing power for 90 days, or there are no credits continuously for 90 days or credits are insufficient to cover interest debited during the period
options.B: The account shows any debit balance at the year-end
options.C: The borrower submits stock statements late on one occasion
options.D: The account has fewer than ten transactions in a quarter

questions.explanation: RBI norms treat a CC/OD account as out of order if the outstanding balance remains continuously in excess of the sanctioned limit or drawing power for 90 days, or where the balance is less than the limit/DP but there are no credits continuously for 90 days as on the balance sheet date or credits are not enough to cover interest debited. An out-of-order account becomes an NPA.

questions.question_text: The Long Form Audit Report (LFAR) in a bank audit is:

options.A: The auditor's report under SA 700 printed in a longer format
options.B: A report required only for co-operative banks under State Acts
options.C: A report prepared by the bank's management for its shareholders
options.D: A report prescribed by the RBI covering matters such as advances, internal controls and compliance, submitted by the auditor in addition to the main audit report

questions.explanation: The LFAR format is prescribed by the RBI and requires auditors to report on specified aspects of the bank's functioning, including advances, cash, investments, compliance with prudential norms and internal controls. It is submitted in addition to the statutory audit report and is not part of the published report.

questions.question_text: A borrower's cash credit account has a sanctioned limit of Rs. 50 lakh. The latest stock statement shows stock of Rs. 80 lakh and unpaid creditors for goods of Rs. 20 lakh. The margin stipulated is 25%. What is the drawing power?

options.A: Rs. 60 lakh
options.B: Rs. 45 lakh
options.C: Rs. 50 lakh
options.D: Rs. 40 lakh

questions.explanation: Paid stock = Rs. 80 lakh - Rs. 20 lakh = Rs. 60 lakh. Drawing power = 60 x (1 - 25%) = Rs. 45 lakh. Since this is below the sanctioned limit of Rs. 50 lakh, the borrower can draw only up to Rs. 45 lakh. Rs. 60 lakh ignores the margin, and Rs. 40 lakh wrongly applies the margin to gross stock before deducting creditors (80 x 75% - 20).

questions.question_text: During the audit of a bank branch, the auditor finds that interest on a loan account classified as NPA has been debited to the account and credited to interest income on an accrual basis. The auditor should:

options.A: Accept the treatment because accrual accounting must always be followed
options.B: Require the unrealised interest to be reversed from income, since income on NPAs is recognised only when actually realised
options.C: Ignore it if the amount is below the branch's materiality
options.D: Require the interest to be shown as an extraordinary item

questions.explanation: Under RBI income recognition norms, interest on NPAs is not recognised on accrual basis but only when actually received. Interest already taken to income on an account that becomes NPA should be reversed if uncollected. The auditor checks that unrealised interest is not included in income.

questions.question_text: To verify balances held by a bank with other banks, the bank auditor should primarily:

options.A: Obtain balance confirmations from the other banks and examine reconciliation statements, investigating old unreconciled entries
options.B: Rely on the branch manager's certificate of balances
options.C: Count the cash in the bank's vaults
options.D: Review the bank's advertisements for interest rates

questions.explanation: Balances with RBI and other banks are verified by obtaining confirmations, comparing them with the books and examining reconciliations. Long-outstanding or unusual reconciling items may indicate errors or frauds and should be investigated. A manager's certificate is internal evidence and less reliable.

questions.question_text: The forms of balance sheet and profit and loss account of a banking company are prescribed in:

options.A: The Third Schedule to the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
options.B: Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013
options.C: The CARO
options.D: The First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949

questions.explanation: Section 29 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 requires banking companies to prepare their balance sheet and profit and loss account in the forms set out in the Third Schedule to that Act. Schedule III to the Companies Act applies to other companies, and its requirements do not override the special form prescribed for banks.

questions.question_text: Just before the year-end, a bank sanctioned a fresh loan to a borrower whose existing account was overdue for more than 90 days, and used the proceeds solely to clear the overdue interest and instalments. The auditor should:

options.A: Classify the account as standard because overdues have been cleared
options.B: Accept the classification but mention it in an Other Matter paragraph
options.C: Treat the arrangement as evergreening, disregard the apparent recovery, and classify the account as NPA
options.D: Treat the fresh loan as an investment

questions.explanation: Funding overdue interest or instalments through fresh or additional loans, without genuine recovery from the borrower's own resources, is evergreening. It conceals the NPA status and inflates income. The auditor should treat the account as NPA, reverse any income recognised from such adjustments and report the matter appropriately.

questions.question_text: The central statutory auditor of a bank receives reports from the auditors of many branches. When using the work of branch auditors, the central auditor should:

options.A: Consider the guidance in SA 600, evaluate the branch auditors' reports, and determine how their findings affect the bank's financial statements as a whole
options.B: Accept the branch reports without considering their findings
options.C: Exclude unaudited branches from the bank's financial statements
options.D: Re-audit every branch personally before signing

questions.explanation: In bank audits, branch audits are performed by branch auditors and the central auditor uses their work. Following SA 600 on using the work of another auditor, the central auditor considers the competence of branch auditors, reviews their reports and LFARs, and evaluates the impact of their observations on the bank's overall financial statements and the audit opinion.

questions.topic: Ethics and Terms of Audit Engagements
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT one of the fundamental principles of the ICAI Code of Ethics?

options.A: Integrity
options.B: Profitability
options.C: Objectivity
options.D: Confidentiality

questions.explanation: The fundamental principles are integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care, confidentiality and professional behaviour. Profitability is a business goal, not an ethical principle, and must never compromise the fundamental principles.

questions.topic: Ethics and Terms of Audit Engagements
questions.question_text: Navya & Associates maintains the books of account of a client and then audits the financial statements prepared from those books. The main threat to independence created is:

options.A: Familiarity threat
options.B: Self-review threat
options.C: Intimidation threat
options.D: Advocacy threat

questions.explanation: A self-review threat arises when the auditor evaluates results of a service previously performed by the auditor's own firm, such as financial statements prepared from records it maintained. The firm may not appropriately evaluate its own work. For company audits, section 144 of the Companies Act, 2013 also prohibits the auditor from rendering accounting and book-keeping services.

questions.topic: Ethics and Terms of Audit Engagements
questions.question_text: CA Mohit has been the engagement partner on the audit of Sundaram Textiles Ltd. for twelve years and regularly holidays with its finance director. The principal threat to his independence is:

options.A: Advocacy threat
options.B: Self-interest threat
options.C: Self-review threat
options.D: Familiarity threat

questions.explanation: A familiarity threat arises when, due to a long or close relationship with a client, the auditor becomes too sympathetic to their interests or too accepting of their work. Long association with a senior client official and close personal relations are classic examples. Safeguards include rotation of the engagement partner.

questions.topic: Ethics and Terms of Audit Engagements
questions.question_text: Under Clause (8) of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, a member in practice is guilty of professional misconduct if he:

options.A: Accepts an audit of a company where the previous auditor has died
options.B: Accepts a position as auditor previously held by another chartered accountant without first communicating with him in writing
options.C: Charges a fee that is lower than the previous auditor's fee
options.D: Accepts an audit of a newly incorporated company

questions.explanation: Clause (8) requires that before accepting a position as auditor previously held by another chartered accountant, the incoming auditor must first communicate with the previous auditor in writing. The purpose is to learn whether there are professional reasons why the appointment should not be accepted. A first audit of a new company has no previous auditor.

questions.topic: Ethics and Terms of Audit Engagements
questions.question_text: CA Pooja agrees to audit a company for a fee equal to 2% of its net profit for the year. This is professional misconduct under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 because:

options.A: It results in sharing of fees with a non-member
options.B: It amounts to charging fees based on a percentage of profits, which Clause (10) of Part I of the First Schedule prohibits except as permitted by the Council's regulations
options.C: The fee is lower than the minimum scale prescribed for audits
options.D: Audit fees can only be fixed by the Central Government

questions.explanation: Clause (10) of Part I of the First Schedule treats it as misconduct if a member in practice charges or offers to charge fees based on a percentage of profits or contingent upon findings or results, except as permitted under regulations (for example, certain receivership or liquidation roles). Fees linked to profits create a self-interest threat to independence.

questions.topic: Ethics and Terms of Audit Engagements
questions.question_text: A practising chartered accountant discloses information about a client's business acquired in the course of an audit to a competitor, without the client's consent and without any legal requirement. This is misconduct under:

options.A: Clause (6) of Part I of the First Schedule
options.B: Clause (8) of Part I of the First Schedule
options.C: Clause (10) of Part I of the Second Schedule
options.D: Clause (1) of Part I of the Second Schedule

questions.explanation: Clause (1) of Part I of the Second Schedule makes it misconduct for a member in practice to disclose information acquired in the course of professional engagement to any person other than the client, without the client's consent or otherwise than as required by law. Clause (6) of the First Schedule concerns solicitation, Clause (8) communication with the previous auditor, and Clause (10) of the Second Schedule client monies.

questions.topic: Ethics and Terms of Audit Engagements
questions.question_text: CA Vikram signs the audit report of a company relying entirely on a working paper prepared by an article assistant on a material inventory balance, without any review. The inventory is later found to be grossly overstated. He is most likely to be held guilty under:

options.A: Clause (12) of Part I of the First Schedule, for allowing a non-member to sign on his behalf
options.B: Clause (2) of Part I of the First Schedule, for sharing fees with a non-member
options.C: Clause (7) of Part I of the Second Schedule, for not exercising due diligence or being grossly negligent in the conduct of professional duties
options.D: Clause (1) of Part I of the Second Schedule, for disclosing client information

questions.explanation: Clause (7) of Part I of the Second Schedule covers a member who does not exercise due diligence or is grossly negligent in conducting professional duties. Signing a report on a material area without reviewing the assistant's work reflects lack of due diligence. Here CA Vikram signed the report himself, so Clause (12) on allowing others to sign does not apply.

questions.topic: Ethics and Terms of Audit Engagements
questions.question_text: Under SA 210, which of the following is a precondition for an audit?

options.A: Payment of the full audit fee in advance
options.B: The absence of any internal control deficiencies
options.C: An undertaking by management that the auditor will issue an unmodified opinion
options.D: The use by management of an acceptable financial reporting framework and management's agreement that it acknowledges its responsibilities

questions.explanation: SA 210 requires the auditor to determine that the financial reporting framework is acceptable and to obtain management's agreement that it acknowledges and understands its responsibility for preparing the financial statements, for internal control and for providing the auditor with access and information. If the preconditions are not present, the auditor shall not accept the engagement unless required by law.

questions.topic: Ethics and Terms of Audit Engagements
questions.question_text: Which of the following persons is disqualified from appointment as auditor of a company under section 141(3) of the Companies Act, 2013?

options.A: A firm whose partners are all practising chartered accountants
options.B: A chartered accountant who is auditor of ten other companies
options.C: A chartered accountant holding one share of an unrelated company
options.D: An officer or employee of the company

questions.explanation: Section 141(3) disqualifies, among others, a body corporate (other than an LLP), an officer or employee of the company, a partner or employee of an officer or employee, persons with certain financial interests or business relationships, and a person in full-time employment elsewhere, or a person who already holds appointment as auditor of more than twenty companies (with certain companies, such as one person companies, dormant companies and small companies, excluded from the count). A firm of practising chartered accountants can be appointed.

questions.topic: Ethics and Terms of Audit Engagements
questions.question_text: Rathi & Co., an audit firm, has completed two consecutive terms of five years each as auditor of a listed company. Under section 139(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, the firm:

options.A: May be re-appointed for a third term of five years with a special resolution
options.B: May continue indefinitely if the audit committee recommends it
options.C: Cannot be re-appointed as auditor of that company for five years from the completion of its second term
options.D: Cannot be re-appointed as auditor of that company ever again

questions.explanation: Under section 139(2), applicable to listed companies and prescribed classes, an individual cannot be appointed for more than one term of five consecutive years and an audit firm for more than two terms of five consecutive years. After this, they are not eligible for re-appointment in that company for five years (the cooling-off period).

questions.topic: Ethics and Terms of Audit Engagements
questions.question_text: The members of Dhara Polymers Ltd. wish to remove the statutory auditor before the expiry of the term. Under section 140(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, this requires:

options.A: A resolution of the board of directors with the auditor's written consent
options.B: A special resolution only, without any government approval
options.C: A special resolution of the company after obtaining the previous approval of the Central Government, and giving the auditor a reasonable opportunity of being heard
options.D: An ordinary resolution passed at a board meeting

questions.explanation: Section 140(1) provides that an auditor appointed under section 139 may be removed before expiry of the term only by a special resolution of the company, after obtaining the previous approval of the Central Government. The auditor concerned must be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard before removal.

questions.topic: Ethics and Terms of Audit Engagements
questions.question_text: The board of Ekta Pharma Ltd. requests its statutory auditor, Sinha & Co., to also conduct its internal audit. Under section 144 of the Companies Act, 2013:

options.A: Sinha & Co. may provide internal audit if approved by the board
options.B: Sinha & Co. may provide internal audit only through a separate firm in which its partners are partners
options.C: Sinha & Co. cannot provide internal audit services to the company, whether directly or indirectly
options.D: Sinha & Co. may provide internal audit if the fee is less than the audit fee

questions.explanation: Section 144 prohibits an auditor from rendering certain services to the company, its holding or subsidiary, directly or indirectly, including accounting and book-keeping, internal audit, design and implementation of financial information systems, actuarial, investment advisory, investment banking, outsourced financial services and management services. Providing them through an associated firm is also covered as 'indirectly'.

questions.topic: Ethics and Terms of Audit Engagements
questions.question_text: The statutory auditor of Gaurav Industries Ltd., a non-government company, resigns mid-term. Under section 139(8) of the Companies Act, 2013, the resulting casual vacancy:

options.A: Is filled by the board alone, with no need for shareholders' approval
options.B: Is filled by the Comptroller and Auditor General within 30 days
options.C: Cannot be filled until the next annual general meeting
options.D: Is filled by the board within 30 days, and the appointment must be approved by the company at a general meeting convened within three months of the board's recommendation

questions.explanation: Section 139(8)(i) provides that a casual vacancy in a non-government company is filled by the board within 30 days. Where the vacancy is caused by resignation, the appointment must also be approved by the company at a general meeting convened within three months of the board's recommendation, and the auditor holds office till the conclusion of the next AGM.
